SBQ1.question: What percentage of the room service cost in Copenhagen comes from the sandwich?
SBQ1.reference_chain: FIND(seg[Copenhagen,Sandwich] | legend[Sandwich]→color[blue], xtick[Copenhagen]) → PROJ(top(seg) → yaxis) → READ(y)≈24.3 → PROJ(top(bar[Copenhagen]) → yaxis) → READ(y)≈46.6 → PCT(24.3, 46.6)≈52 → ANSWER(52)
SBQ1.notes: No participant in this group got the item right. The dominant failure (11/20) is reading the dollar height of the Copenhagen sandwich segment (~24) off the $ y-axis and reporting it as the percentage, with no division by the bar total; a long horizontal line from the y-axis to the sandwich top is the signature sketch. The few who did read the total (~47) and form a ratio made arithmetic or estimation errors (45, 59, 60). The pivotal elements are the top of the whole Copenhagen bar (the denominator) and the sandwich-segment top; one participant even missed the title and said room service was not in the chart.

SBQ2.question: In which city is the cost of soda the highest?
SBQ2.reference_chain: FIND({seg[*,Soda]} | legend[Soda]→color[green]) → SCAN({seg[*,Soda]}) → CMPvis(len(seg[Stockholm,Soda]) > len(seg[Seoul,Soda]) > ...) → ARGMAX({seg[*,Soda]}, len)=Stockholm (≈53.3−43.8≈9.5) → ANSWER(Stockholm)
SBQ2.notes: Every answer in this group was wrong; 13/18 chose Helsinki because its soda segment sits highest on the y-axis (~63), i.e. they ranked the cumulative top position of the green segment rather than its length. Sketches show this clearly: circles on the Helsinki soda segment, lines from its top to the y-axis, or a horizontal line at ~63 across all bars. Two participants used the total Helsinki bar height (one by mistaking brown/Vodka for soda), and only one person compared segment lengths (Stockholm) but then picked the "impossible" option. The pivotal element is len(seg[*,Soda]), which requires SEG(top − bottom) on non-aligned baselines.

SBQ3.question: The cost of vodka in Helsinki is higher than that of Toronto.
SBQ3.reference_chain: FIND(seg[Helsinki,Vodka] | legend[Vodka]→color[orange], xtick[Helsinki]) → FIND(seg[Toronto,Vodka]) → SEG(68.6 − 63.1)≈5.5 → SEG(55.8 − 47.8)≈8 → CMP(5.5 < 8) → ANSWER(False)
SBQ3.notes: Accuracy split roughly in half (20/42 correct). The decisive split is the operand: people who compared the LENGTH of the two orange vodka segments (visually, with brackets/I-beams, or by projecting top and bottom edges to the axis and subtracting) answered False, while those who compared where the segments sit (top of the Helsinki bar at ~68.5 vs Toronto at ~56), often drawing a horizontal line across from Helsinki's top, answered True. A notable minority (5) explicitly could not decide whether the segment length or the cumulative height encodes vodka cost and chose Impossible/not sure. The non-adjacent bars and offset baselines make the length comparison hard, and one person marked the soda segments instead.

new_symbols.extent(m): the vertical span [bottom, top] of a mark, used when translating a segment to compare against another
new_symbols.PROJ(e → right/across): projection drawn horizontally away from the y-axis or across to another bar rather than to the axis

SBQ4.notes: Most participants (28/42) got this right, largely because the item is forgiving: N.Y.C. soda and water segments look about equal while Stockholm soda is obviously longer, so a quick per-city visual length comparison (or an explicit 1:1 vs ~2-3:1 estimate) suffices. Several people reasoned with differences instead of ratios; this happens to give the right answer for Stockholm, but it misleads when the "gap" is the vertical distance between segments (the intervening peanut band), which led to True. Others projected cumulative segment tops to the axis, compared only one of the two items, or gave up ("not sure") because of the four operands across two non-adjacent bars. The few who did subtract (top − bottom) snapped to the 35 and 40 ticks and got 5, or misread the 5-unit gridline step and got 11.
